newsitem.title: GERMANY: Private sectors seeks self-regulation of Internet.
newsitem.headline: Private sectors seeks self-regulation of Internet.

text.p: Private sector representatives urged a conference of government ministers on Monday to let cyberspace companies answer security, privacy and social questions posed by the exploding information society.
They said government ministers should regulate the Internet with a "light hand."
Customers are already forcing online service providers and other companies to secure personal and financial data and restrict illegal content like child pornography, even without government mandates.

"Our consumer customers want us to give them protection against child pornography," said George Vradenburg, senior vice president of America Online Inc. "Businesses are demanding that we make electronic commerce secure."
Klaus Mangold, head of the financial services unit of German car maker Daimler-Benz AG, said "many of these issues will be answered without governments taking action."
Mangold said his unit, Daimler-Benz InterServices AG (Debis), had to provide security to succeed in electronic commerce.
Tightly regulating cyberspace could stifle "an explosion of human development" sparked by the Inernet in the next century, Vradenburg said.

"We can and must break the regulatory cycle that has trapped each new electronic medium in this century," he said. "It is clear that Internet growth will be driven by those who use and build it and that government will have and should have a lesser role."
Canadian Industry Minister John Manley told reporters no government was capable of controlling the development of cyberspace.
"Public sector is unable to contemplate wisely the regulative or legislative rules that need to be in place when development is as rapid as it is," he said.
But some government ministers said they were not yet willing to trust industry alone to shape something as far-reaching and powerful as the Internet.

"There has to be basic principles set out," said German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, who as co-host helped bring ministers from more than 40 nations to Germany for the two-day "Global Information Networks" conference.

Private sector representatives also called for governments to move more vigorously to allow competition in their telecommunications markets and liberalise regulations on powerful encryption technology that protects credit card numbers and other financial data needed for Internet commerce.
